description: María Isabel Vélez, Analista de datos. Medellín, Colombia.
summary: Planetary Mirrors asks a simple question from my country: does Colombia have terrain that resembles the places where NASA plans to land near the Moon’s south pole? Using NASA open data (NASADEM for Earth and LRO/LOLA slope maps for the Moon) at the same 80 m resolution, I measured the slope distribution of 15 km windows and compared five Colombian zones with seven Artemis III candidate regions using a simple similarity distance. Puracé volcano is the closest match in slope distribution, with Nevado del Ruiz a close second, while the flattest zones (Tatacoa and La Guajira) are the least similar: flat is not the same as analogous. The method uses only open data, runs in Google Colab and can be repeated in any country to find new Earth analogs for lunar exploration.
details:
What it does. Planetary Mirrors tests whether Colombia has terrain that resembles the regions NASA is considering for landing near the Moon's south pole (the Artemis III candidate regions). Instead of looking for places that merely look like the Moon, it compares the distribution of slopes of each place.

How it works. (1) I use ~15 km windows: seven Artemis III candidate regions on the Moon and five zones in Colombia (Puracé volcano, Nevado del Ruiz, Chicamocha canyon, Tatacoa desert and La Guajira). (2) For Colombia I read NASADEM elevation (NASA/JPL), average it to 80 m and compute the slope of every pixel; for the Moon I read the LRO/LOLA slope map (NASA) at the same 80 m. (3) Each window becomes a "slope profile": the percentage of terrain in six slope classes (0-5, 5-8, 8-10, 10-15, 15-30 and >30 degrees); NASA's lander tolerance is about 8 degrees. (4) Similarity is a simple distance: the percentage of terrain that would have to change class for two windows to be identical. (5) To judge whether a distance is large or small, I also measure how different the Artemis regions are from each other, and I test robustness by shifting each Colombian window about 5 km in four directions.

Findings. Puracé is the most similar zone (median distance 18.7, inside the 5 to 53 range found among the Artemis regions themselves, whose median is 22.3). Nevado del Ruiz is a close second, and the flattest zones, Tatacoa and La Guajira, are the least similar. Flat is not the same as analogous, because the candidate regions are crater rims and massifs, not plains. The ranking at the extremes is stable when windows are shifted; first place is contested between Puracé and Nevado del Ruiz.

Why it matters. It offers a transparent, reproducible way to screen Earth sites for rover and lander navigation tests, it relies only on open data, and it can be repeated in any country. It also shows that a country without well-known analog sites may still have candidates.

Tools. Python (rasterio, pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, pystac-client), Google Colab, NASADEM through the Microsoft Planetary Computer, and NASA PGDA LRO/LOLA products.

Limits of the analogy. Earth cannot reproduce lunar gravity, vacuum or radiation. Similar slopes do not mean similar geology (Puracé is a volcano; lunar slopes come mostly from impact craters). Only 7 of the 13 regions could be measured, with approximate centers; 80 m pixels smooth small features; and there is one window per zone.

Use of AI. The research question, the choice of the Moon, the site criteria, the choice of Colombian zones and the interpretation of results are mine. I used Claude (Anthropic) as a mentor that asked guiding questions and as a coding assistant for the Python code and the suggested similarity metric. I ran and checked all analyses myself; this is also stated in the notebook.
